opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think energy and climate are among the most important areas where AI could make a real difference, and I'd put them right up there with biology and medicine. I see it working on a few different levels.

The most immediate one is efficiency. A lot of our existing infrastructure, things like power grids, data centers, and industrial processes, runs far from optimally. These are complex systems with huge numbers of interacting variables, which is exactly what modern machine learning is good at modeling and optimizing. We saw this early on when we applied our systems to data center cooling and got significant reductions in the energy used. You could imagine that kind of approach applied across national grids, balancing intermittent renewables like wind and solar, predicting demand and supply, and reducing waste everywhere. Each of those gains might be ten or twenty percent, but at global scale that's enormous.

The second level, which excites me even more, is using AI as a tool for scientific discovery to find genuinely new solutions. Materials science is a great example. If you want better batteries, better solar cells, superconductors, or more efficient catalysts for things like carbon capture or green hydrogen, you're essentially searching an astronomically large space of possible compounds and structures. That's very similar to the protein folding problem: a vast combinatorial space where you need good models to guide the search. With AlphaFold we showed that if you build the right kind of system, you can turn what was a decades-long experimental slog into something you can do computationally in seconds. I'd love to see that happen for materials.

Then there's fusion, which I think is one of the most exciting long-term possibilities. We worked on controlling the plasma in a tokamak using reinforcement learning, holding the plasma in different shapes with the magnetic coils. Containing a plasma hotter than the sun is an incredibly hard control problem, and it turns out learning systems can be very good at it. If AI can help accelerate the path to practical fusion, or, alongside better solar and storage, help us reach effectively abundant clean energy, that changes everything. So many other problems, like water desalination, cleaning up the atmosphere, and even some economic and geopolitical tensions, become much more tractable if energy becomes cheap and clean.

And finally there's climate modeling itself. Weather and climate prediction are incredibly complex, and we've seen learned models start to match or beat traditional numerical methods on some forecasting tasks, while running much faster. Better predictions help with adaptation, things like preparing for extreme weather and planning agriculture.

Of course people rightly point out that AI itself uses a lot of energy, and we need to take that seriously and keep making our systems more efficient. But I'm fairly confident that the gains AI can deliver for energy and climate will vastly outweigh its own footprint. If you think of AI as the ultimate tool for accelerating science, then climate and energy are exactly the kind of grand challenges it should be pointed at.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI-guided materials discovery as a way to find new batteries, solar cells, and catalysts that could advance clean energy and climate solutions.

r002.rationale: The response discusses near-term efficiency gains and current forecasting progress, but does not predict that AI will materially help solve these problems within roughly five years.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is one of the areas I'm most optimistic about, actually. If you look at the big problems in energy and climate, a lot of them are fundamentally science problems, and they're the kind of science problems that have been stuck for a long time because the search spaces are just enormous. Things like room-temperature superconductors, better battery chemistries, new catalysts for carbon capture, materials for more efficient solar cells. In each of these cases, the number of possible materials or molecules you could try is astronomically large, and humans have really only explored a tiny corner of it through trial and error over decades.

What we saw with AlphaFold is that if you can get the right kind of model, you can collapse a problem that took the field fifty years into something you can do in an afternoon. And I think materials science is the next obvious place for that. We've already done some early work there with GNoME, where we predicted on the order of two million new crystal structures, hundreds of thousands of which look stable. That's more than all the stable materials humanity had discovered in the whole of history up to that point. Now, prediction is only the first step. You then have to synthesize them, test them, and that's where the loop with experimental labs becomes really important. But the point is, AI can act as a kind of filter or a guide, so instead of searching blindly you're searching in the most promising regions.

Then there's fusion, which I find incredibly exciting. We did a collaboration with the Swiss Plasma Center where we used reinforcement learning to control the plasma in a tokamak. Controlling the magnetic fields to keep the plasma stable is this very hard real-time control problem, and it turns out it's quite similar in spirit to the kinds of things we did with games, in the sense that you have a system with many degrees of freedom and you need a policy that acts in milliseconds. That was a nice demonstration that these techniques transfer out of the simulated world into real physical systems.

And then there's a more mundane but actually very large impact category, which is just efficiency. We used AI to reduce the energy used for cooling in Google's data centers by something like forty percent. That's not glamorous, but if you apply that kind of optimization across grids, across buildings, across industrial processes, logistics, it adds up to a huge amount. Weather forecasting is another one. Our GraphCast model outperforms the traditional numerical methods on most metrics and it does it in under a minute on a single machine, rather than hours on a supercomputer. Better forecasting matters directly for integrating renewables, because wind and solar are intermittent, and if you can predict them better you can manage the grid better.

So I'd put it in two buckets. There's the near-term stuff, which is optimization and prediction, and that's happening now. And then there's the longer-term, more transformative stuff, which is using AI to actually accelerate the fundamental science so we discover the new materials and new energy sources we need. I think if we get AGI right, that second bucket could be one of the most important things it does for humanity. Energy abundance changes almost every other problem, including water, food, and lifting people out of poverty. That's really the goal.

r002.rationale: It says optimization and prediction are happening now and describes longer-term scientific advances, but gives no prediction that AI will materially help solve these problems within roughly five years.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s enormous potential. Energy and climate involve some very difficult scientific and engineering problems, and AI can help us explore possible solutions much more efficiently.

One part is improving the systems we already have: reducing the energy needed to cool buildings, making electricity grids more efficient, or helping us predict supply and demand when we have more wind and solar power. Those improvements may seem incremental, but at scale they can make a substantial difference.

Then there’s the discovery side. Could we find better materials for batteries, cheaper catalysts, or more efficient solar cells? Could AI help us understand and control the plasma in a fusion reactor? These are areas where searching through a vast space of possibilities, and learning from simulations and experiments, could be incredibly useful.

Of course, AI itself consumes energy, so we have to account for that honestly. And discovering something in a computer is only part of the challenge—you still have to build it, test it, and deploy it. But I’m optimistic that AI can become a powerful tool for the scientists and engineers working on these problems.

r001.rationale: The response names AI-assisted discovery of better batteries, catalysts, and solar cells, but does not identify it as a route to revolutionary advances in climate and energy use.

r002.rationale: The response expresses optimism that AI can help, but gives no prediction about material help within roughly five years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s enormous potential. Energy and climate are areas where we have very clear problems to solve, and AI can help us explore the space of possible solutions much faster.

One example is making the systems we already have more efficient—using less energy to cool a data centre, or helping balance an electricity grid as more wind and solar come online. Those are complex prediction and optimisation problems, which are a natural fit for AI.

Then there’s the scientific discovery side: finding better battery materials, better catalysts, or helping us understand and control plasma for fusion. What excites me is the possibility of using AI to build better models of these systems, propose an experiment, learn from the result, and repeat that cycle much more quickly.

Of course, AI itself consumes energy, so we have to take that seriously. And discovering a material isn’t the same as manufacturing it cheaply at scale. But I think AI could become an extraordinarily useful tool for the scientists and engineers working on those bottlenecks.

r001.rationale: The response mentions AI-assisted discovery of better battery materials and catalysts, but does not identify it as a route to revolutionary advances in climate and energy use.

r002.rationale: The response gives no prediction or timeframe of roughly five years for AI materially helping solve energy and climate problems.
